All non-irrelevant documents (d1-d5) agree on the core claim: standing desks are better for health than prolonged sitting, as they reduce sedentary time and are linked to benefits like burning more calories, lowering blood sugar, and reducing back pain and disease risk [d1, d2, d3, d4]. The evidence uniformly supports the answer. d1, d2, and d4 cite specific benefits like calorie burn and reduced disease risk [d1, d2, d4]. d3 and d5 emphasize that movement and alternating postures are key, aligning with the benefits of standing desks over static sitting [d3, d5]. Together, they provide a consistent, non-contradictory case.

Based on the retrieved evidence, standing desks are generally better for health than prolonged sitting. Using a standing desk reduces sedentary time, which is linked to lower risks of obesity, heart disease, and diabetes [d1, d2, d3]. Standing burns more calories than sitting and can help lower blood sugar spikes after meals [d2, d4]. It also encourages movement and can reduce back pain, though alternating between sitting and standing is recommended for optimal benefit [d1, d3, d5].
